hints: Look closely at the two curves. Which peak is lower, and what does an enzyme do to the height of the energy barrier?
Remember activation energy is measured upwards from the starting substrate energy level to the top of the peak for that pathway, not from the products.
walkthrough:
**Spot the two pathways**

Think of this like two hills to climb. The tall hill is the reaction without an enzyme. The short hill is the reaction with an enzyme, because enzymes lower the barrier.

So focus only on the lower peak for this question.

**Recall what activation energy means**

Activation energy is the extra energy the substrates need to reach the top (the transition state). It is always measured from the substrate starting level up to the peak.

$$Activation\ energy = peak\ energy - substrate\ energy$$

**Read arrow 2 on the graph**

Arrow 2 starts exactly at the substrate energy line and stops exactly at the top of the lower (enzyme) peak. That is the new, lowered activation energy.

Arrow 1 is just how much the enzyme lowered the barrier. So 1 + 2 together would be the old, higher barrier without enzyme.

options.A: 1 + 2 is the distance from substrates to the top of the tall peak, so this is the activation energy without the enzyme, not with it.
options.B: 2 only goes from the substrate level to the top of the lower enzyme peak, which is exactly the lowered activation energy.
options.C: 3 - 2 does not measure a barrier from substrates to a peak, it mixes a measurement from products (3) with one from substrates (2).
options.D: 4 goes from the product level up to the tall peak, so it is not an activation energy measured from the substrates.
